#40883. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1018 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.
  • The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also highlights that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.
  • These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also highlights that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors.

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health complications (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

It has been revealed that other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”.

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

Industry observers note that “Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view newly introduced symptoms through that same lens.”.

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are key, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a initiative for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

In a recent development, carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he stated.

Industry News: Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive.
  • It comes just four days after Elon Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.
  • UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company states it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The organization publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.

It comes just four days after Elon Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.

UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company states it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.

In exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the organization wrote.

UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.

And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP claims it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.

The post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.

UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the firm’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.

It has been revealed that musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He stated Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

If the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.

As we reported when Tesla revealed the wind-down, that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.

It has been revealed that the real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks, a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.

Industry observers note that even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data indicated SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, launched a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August. None of it fixed demand.

Sources indicate that I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.

Of course, it’s more complicated than that.

There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.

First off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.

Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.

In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.

Sources indicate that I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

Who is singing up to light their cash on fire? There is just no way that would work. Unless Tesla just gave them the designs and tooling. Then they are stuck the same problem with who is their market. There are 3 ev trucks coming that are cheaper better and more practical. Likey 3 or 4 more by the end of the decade.

Sources indicate that you could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too massive a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid.

If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the manufacturer to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.

But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

#40880. Industry News: Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it.
  • Sources indicate that humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing.
  • Recent findings suggest that to probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Sources indicate that humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some new research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

Recent findings suggest that to probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

The team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

If blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

“In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, mentioned in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”.

Industry observers note that the team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

Sources indicate that the researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely latest call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”.

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

Recent findings suggest that “One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”.

#40878. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (596 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes.
  • That stated, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues.
  • “The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” remarked Upcoming York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

That stated, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” remarked Upcoming York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

Recent findings suggest that the Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence shows that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

It has been revealed that previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these significant ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” said Snyder.

According to recent reports, klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

The study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

It has been revealed that “This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”.

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the living room, a painting by Cecily Brown hangs above a Joel Shapiro table with sculptures by Jonathan Borofsky (left) and Ivy Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson (right), beside a Southeast Asian sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that describing the allure of her sprawling prewar Manhattan apartment, art adviser Ivy Shapiro returns to one theme again and again. “It’s old-school,” she insists. “I have this fantasy that I’m living in a different era. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.
  • This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

Recent findings suggest that it is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

Sources indicate that the researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

In a recent development, MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

In a recent development, ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Industry observers note that research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion stated that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly crucial at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

In a recent development, ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:.

Recent findings suggest that “These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross remarked.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it. Yet for years, prostate cancer screening via the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test has been plagued by vague recommendations, and some back-and-forth messaging that flipped between “get it” and “the benefits might not be worth it.” Until recently, organizations including the American Cancer Society (ACS) used to give a recommendation that at age 50, guys should talk with their doctors about screening, then engage in a process of “shared decision-making” about whether to get the test.

Many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not. Without a clear recommendation, it was easy for some to think this PSA blood test wasn’t very important to do at all. The landscape has changed.

It has been revealed that the American Cancer Society just came out with upcoming guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test. Guys at average risk should start at age 50. Guys at higher risk (more on that later) should start at 45.

Why that’s a significant deal: “The new guideline not only gets rid of shared decision-making, which is really difficult to execute, is subject to bias, and is really time-intensive,” says Yaw Nyame, MD, of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center at the University of Washington Medical Center. “But it couples that with a better understanding of what present-day prostate cancer screening is.”.

Sources indicate that today, the PSA test is “just the first step, not the final answer,” claims William Dahut, MD, chief scientific officer at ACS, and a contributing author to the guidelines. “It is a simple blood test, and an elevated result does not automatically mean cancer of the need for a biopsy.” Many more tools including MRIs and biomarkers help physicians drill down on who needs additional testing. “Our goal is to find prostate cancer earlier, while avoiding unnecessary procedures and treatment,” Dr. Dahut adds.

What changed that prompted the revised recommendations? “It’s key to understand that guidance evolves as the evidence does,” says Dr. Dahut. Research has piled up to indicate that PSA screening reduces prostate cancer deaths.

Industry observers note that “We do not need to make a disclaimer that maybe you should, maybe you shouldn’t do it. Everyone should do it and you should start early, especially if you have a higher risk of cancer,” notes Dr. Nyame, who was on the expert panel that reviewed the new ACS screening guidelines.

Sources indicate that while all men should get the test, according to the fresh guidelines, it’s not a “one size fits all” screening recommendation, Dr. Nyame explains. Recommendations vary according to risk. Find your category and screen according to that.

These are the new ACS guidelines for who and when:.

Sources indicate that other prostate screening guidelines came out earlier in 2026 from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society for Urologic Oncology (SUO) that had slightly different recommendations for the age at which you should start screening. What gives? The difference in recommended age and frequency of screening “has to do with how the guideline creators are viewing the different studies that they’re using to support their decision making,” Dr. Nyame claims.

Sources indicate that it doesn’t mean guys should throw up their hands and do nothing in frustration. “The AUA/SUO and ACS guidelines recognize the benefit of knowing a PSA test result earlier in life. A PSA test in the 40- to 50-year age range is a good predictor of the likelihood someone has or will develop a clinically significant prostate cancer,” states James A. Eastham, MD, chief of the urology service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. A higher level early in life is a strong signal that you need to be really diligent about checking your PSA.

“We’ve watched prostate cancer incidence increase—especially metastatic cancer, for over a decade now,” claims Dr. Nyame. “And to know that we have a guideline that is so action-oriented toward reversing that course is really exciting.”.

#40872. When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind

When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.
  • According to recent reports, I once sat in a room while a psychiatrist discussed with my parents his belief that I would face a lifetime of institutionalization.
  • Sources indicate that I borrow this term from biologist and natural philosopher Michael Levin: Mind-blindness is the inability to recognize the minds of others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 18, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

According to recent reports, I once sat in a room while a psychiatrist discussed with my parents his belief that I would face a lifetime of institutionalization. At 15, I was perfectly capable of understanding him. The conversation excluded me not because I couldn’t grasp it but because that doctor had uttered the word “schizophrenia.” Once he did, the sense that anything real might exist in my head, even the most basic sense, evaporated.

The people around me became mind-blind.

Sources indicate that I borrow this term from biologist and natural philosopher Michael Levin: Mind-blindness is the inability to recognize the minds of others. Michael was gracious enough to chat with me about it. He believes humans exist in a world full of minds, with cognition a potential not just for other creatures, but for cells, large language models, even algorithms.

“We tend to think of things as either dumb like rocks or smart like humans and angels,” Levin said. Instead, Levin believes that the sciences of cybernetics and the tools of behavior science now show mind exists on a continuum, involving testable traits like whether a being can learn and what its competencies are.

Mind-Blindness Begins With Other Humans.

As Levin puts it, it’s more a question of what kind of intelligence exists, and how much, than a yes-or-no distinction.

When I told Michael Levin I believed humans’ mind-blindness begins with other humans, he said, “You’re absolutely right.” And he added, “I think the problem is a scarcity mentality with respect to compassion. It’s as if people thought, if we allow too many into the club of cognition, there will not be enough care or love for me.”.

I once spoke in sign language with an orangutan named Chantek, who indicated he found his cage mate Sibu a bit messy. Remembering the thoughtfulness of his eyes still makes seeing a caged animal unbearable to me. I live with two cats who often let me know, with headbutts and meows, that I’m about to get sick before I know it; I know we overlook the capacities of the beings around us.

And humans can be highly mind-blind to each other.

It has been revealed that white Europeans have historically demonstrated mind-blindness to other racial groups, to the point of enslaving them. Jeffrey Epstein was mind-blind to women, which no doubt made him feel better about his abuse. And based on their testimony, Lindsay Clancy’s caregivers remained mind-blind to the actual thoughts she was having. They slotted her pain into symptom categories, missing the awful acts her mind pushed her toward.

Industry observers note that psychiatry, and the culture that accepts its premises, has been mind-blind. This isn’t only true of my early doctor. Autistic people have suffered with the stigma that they lack “theory of mind,” or an understanding that the people around them have minds and feelings.

When I taught, fellow professors often shared their conviction that students who bothered them must be “on the spectrum.” Though “spectrum” has gotten to be a shorthand for a jumble of traits that don’t even fit together: insensitivity, oversensitivity, bluntness, shyness. These biases still lead to real discrimination, though they’re based largely on misunderstandings of subtle differences.

Then there is the child I was, turned to vapor by the word “schizophrenia.” My diagnosis changed ultimately. But I would be who I am with or without a word from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual next to my name.

Mental states, which DSM terms try and fail to pin down, are less hardwired, binary differences between people than they are part of the human condition, one piece of all our potential. They reflect inborn flaws less than they show the tumult of living a life in this human body.

Sources indicate that A good share of the population—as many as 15 percent or more of adults—will at some point in their lives hear voices. Up to 38 percent will experience visual hallucinations, a high enough number to suggest this alone shouldn’t be enough to diagnose psychosis, though it very well could be. And one-quarter to one-third of people who have what is diagnosed as a full-blown schizophrenic episode will never have another one. Those whose conditions become chronic may be impaired as much or more by the treatment as the underlying mental state.

Trauma makes the experience of psychosis far more likely, certainly a factor for me as a girl. Difficult life experiences can also plant the seeds of creativity and novel thought. This was true of mind pioneer Carl Jung. An early exposure to death, and later sexual abuse, traumatized Jung, and as an adult he had an extended period of hallucinations.

Jung described “incessant visions” in his Red Book and compared their impact to thunderstorms and floods. Though this period wasn’t a pointless bout of “illness” in Jung’s life—he called that time the root of his most vital ideas, such as the existence of archetypes and the collective unconscious.

Recent findings suggest that michael Levin has more to offer the field of psychiatry than the helpful idea of mind-blindness. He believes that in the future we might practice a somatic psychiatry that exploits bioelectricity, the “cognitive glue” aligning cells toward organ-scale anatomical goals, using bioelectrical signaling as an interface through which to communicate desired healthy form and function.

Levin also told me, “Our cells provide another level of intelligence in the body,” and communicating at these other levels might offer pathways to mind care.

Before we fully understand the many ways we can help ourselves, we need to drop narrow beliefs about minds.

Carl Jung wrote that our inner worlds are “truly infinite, in no way poorer than the outer one,” so powerful and individual that “humans live in two worlds.” We share the former world with a dizzying array of other beings. Perhaps, in ways that are not always easy to understand, we share the inner world as well.

“What I hope is that when we can acknowledge that the mind can belong to things that don’t look anything like us,” Michael Levin told me, “our differences become laughably small.”.

According to recent reports, dermatologists say there's something to this. "Your lymph system helps move excess waste and fluid throughout the body," explains Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research at Mount Sinai Hospital. "Lymphatic massages help enhance activity of the system to circulate excess fluid and depuff.".

Sources indicate that doctors may recommend lymphatic drainage massage to people with health conditions like lymphedema or to post-surgical patients, claims Ife J. Rodney, MD, founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics. For everyone else, the data is less clear on whether lymphatic drainage offers much benefit.

Sources indicate that "For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement, though research on gua sha is limited," Dr. Rodney says. Note the "temporary" part of what she stated. Despite what you may hear on social media, lymphatic drainage won't permanently alter your cheekbones and jawline, although Dr. Rodney says this may help your skin look fresher and your features look more defined. "Think of it as an optional self-care step, not a requirement for healthy skin," Dr. Rodney says.

Want to opt into this? There is a range of tools to consider—and doctors say you don't need to spend a ton to get results.

A gua sha tool needs to have at least one smooth edge for lymphatic drainage. But Face Gym's Multi-Sculpt High-Performance Contouring Tool has six different edges to focus on different areas of your face. Long and medium smooth edges are made for classic lymphatic drainage, while shorter sides are ideal for areas around your eyes. The tool even includes rounded teeth for fine lines and a targeted tip for acupressure. (Face Gym has an instructional video to help guide you through all of this.).

Sources indicate that face Gym's gua sha tool is made from stainless steel, which is hypoallergenic and easy to clean. The stainless-steel tool is easy to clean, but any product can irritate skin. It also has a nice cooling effect after briefly popping it into the fridge. While this gua sha tool is on the pricier end, its stainless steel construction means it won't shatter like its crystal counterparts if you accidentally drop it.

In a recent development, both are used for facial massage, but a roller moves across the skin by rolling, while gua sha uses sweeping strokes with a smooth-edged tool. You simply glide the roller across your face with gentle pressure to support lymphatic drainage. This is another stainless steel tool, which means it's a little more hygienic and easy to clean than its more traditional crystal versions. It's also highly likely to survive in the event of a drop.

The stainless steel has a natural cooling feel against the skin, although you can toss it in the fridge for extra chilliness. This tool is heavier than stone or crystal rollers—keep that on the back burner if you're used to those. It also pairs best with an oil or serum to help it glide smoothly over your skin, so plan to moisturize at the same time.

Dry brushing has the combined benefit of supporting lymphatic drainage and exfoliation at once. But some brushes have stiff bristles that can feel intense—and even irritating—against the skin. Esker's dry brush is gentle against the skin, but still feels firm enough to get things moving.

Esker's dry brush has a spa-like feel, along with an ergonomic design that's easy to grip. It's relatively petite, too, making it easy to toss in a bag for travel or trips to the gym. The only downside of that is the handle isn't long enough to reach your back. (That's more of an exfoliation matter vs. a lymphatic drainage problem, though.) The rules of lymphatic drainage still apply with a brush like this—if it feels irritating to your skin, stop. But if dry brushing is something you're into and you want to try lymphatic drainage on areas of your body other than your face, this is a solid choice.

Most people do gua sha on their face with a sculpting stone, crystal, or steel device. But not everyone is into the sensation of moving something hard across the sensitive skin in that area. Skin Gym answers the call with a face brush designed specifically for gua sha.

Recent findings suggest that the brush is densely packed with soft bristles, creating a feel like you're swiping a really good makeup brush over your skin. It has an ergonomic shape, making it easy to glide over the contours of your face. This brush is pretty beginner-friendly, making it a good entry point if you're gua sha-curious. But be aware that you may not be able to get as much pressure on your skin (if that's even your thing) as you would with a stone or other hard tool. The brush also requires regular cleaning to avoid pushing dirt around your face.

Let's get this out of the way upfront: Vibration plates are a controversial tool. Many make bold claims, like that they can support weight loss or mimic the effects of exercise—those are unfounded. But these plates can improve circulation and lymphatic drainage as a result, as Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise scientist based in Athens, Georgia, previously told Women's Health.

Industry observers note that FWIW, research suggests that you'll get many of the same circulation- (and lymph-)promoting effects from exercise. But if a vibrating plate is more your speed, the LifePro Waver is worth a look. This machine offers 99 speed levels to allow you to fine-tune the intensity. The motor is also quiet, so you don't have to stress about waking up other people in your home. This plate comes with resistance bands and free online workout videos, too. Just be aware that vibration plates aren't safe for everyone—you should take a pass if you're pregnant, prone to blood clots, or struggle with dizziness, for example. Bachelorette star Gabby Windey also recently shared that she broke her back after cranking up her (unnamed) vibrating plate in the name of lymphatic drainage. Though her account is an individual anecdote and doesn’t establish the typical risk, proceed with caution. But if you're looking for a way to get lymphatic drainage moving around your whole body, this is worth considering.

The best type of lymphatic drainage tool for you depends on where you plan to use it on your body. "These types of massages can be performed anywhere, but are extremely common on the face," Dr. Zeichner notes. "Oftentimes, a smooth, but firm tool like gua sha is used.".

A roller is another option for facial lymphatic drainage, and is usually considered more gentle than gua sha. For lymphatic drainage other than the face, some people reach for dry brushes and vibration plates.

For gua sha, Dr. Rodney suggests choosing a tool with smooth, rounded edges with no sharp spots, chips, or cracks. "It should be comfortable to hold and easy to clean," she claims—and that applies to all lymphatic drainage tools. For gua sha and rollers, "you don't need an expensive crystal," Dr. Rodney says.

Dry brushes should also have natural fibers, since synthetic can feel harsh against the skin. Overall, "a smooth finish and gentle technique matter more than the price tag," Dr. Rodney says.

There's no exact weight for a lymphatic drainage tool that's best for everyone. Instead, it should feel substantial in your hand—but not too heavy or too light. You want to be able to comfortably use your tool, and allow the tool to apply pressure vs. heavy force from you.

According to recent reports, they may temporarily reduce puffiness for some people, but evidence for at-home tools and broader health benefits is limited. "For everyday facial puffiness, gentle massage may offer temporary improvement," Dr. Rodney claims. Dr. Zeichner agrees. "Especially if you wake up puffy in the morning after drinking too much alcohol, not having enough sleep, taking in too much salt, or during your menstrual cycle, lymphatic massages can be a useful tool," he says. Just keep in mind that the effects are temporary.

In a recent development, every type of tool is slightly different. "The goal of a lymphatic massage is to improve the body's drainage system," Dr. Zeichner says. "That is why the massage should be performed in a particular way." If you're massaging your face, the pressure should start near the center of your face, before moving out and down toward your collarbones. This follows the natural lymphatic flow, Dr. Zeichner says.

"A few minutes is enough to start," Dr. Rodney indicates. "Keep the pressure light—bruising is a sign to stop, not a sign it’s working.".

It has been revealed that dermatologists recommend taking a pass on lymphatic drainage tools if your skin is irritated, infected, sunburned, or broken. (That includes inflamed acne, eczema, or rosacea flares, per Dr. Rodney.).

Dr. Rodney also suggests checking with your doctor if you take blood thinners, bruise easily, or have blood clots, heart or kidney failure, lymphedema, or a history of cancer treatment or lymph node removal. "After cosmetic procedures or surgery, get clearance from your treating clinician," she says. "Persistent or painful swelling needs an explanation before it needs a massage.".

Latest Update: Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • Sources indicate that UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

Sources indicate that UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

It has been revealed that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

Sources indicate that they measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

It has been revealed that the researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Sources indicate that among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

It has been revealed that when the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is notable to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” stated Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

According to recent reports, these findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” stated Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more vital to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She remarked that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is notable to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
  • I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub.
  • The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

The Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

And a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

According to recent reports, the beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

And Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Recent findings suggest that even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

There are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

Sources indicate that the Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

Industry observers note that and perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

My mum's old Honda-50 (the original cub, early 70's) had a tank that held less than a gallon of petrol. Range was realistically about 50 miles, but no-one even thought about that, it never ran out.

She traded for a honda-90, then a bunch of other stuff, I miss that 90, even now.

But the point is that range is not the concern, very few trips on these are more than 10 - 15 miles, say 30km round-trip.

But the real range, on a battery vehicle, is only about 2/3 of the claim,.

so if the claim is 80, it'll maybe do 55?

Thats enough, if it has the zip to handle traffic, and cruise at 45 - 50mph.

Recent findings suggest that honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

So here I am once again, Honda.

You’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

In medieval Italy, a spider bite could send you into a dancing frenzy

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a chance that if you visited southern Italy during the Middle Ages, you might happen upon a port town where people were dancing uncontrollably in the streets.
  • “Some people say that the bite of a spider caused people to tremor and shake,” Anna Harsh, a professional dancer and founder of the Allegro Dance Company, which specializes in Italian folk dances, tells Popular Science.
  • Tarantism, a historical psychological and social phenomenon that led to anxiety, melancholia, and uncontrollable movement, ran rapidly throughout southern Italy from the 11th to the 17th century.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a chance that if you visited southern Italy during the Middle Ages, you might happen upon a port town where people were dancing uncontrollably in the streets. You’d find them frantically spinning, jumping…even crawling on the ground. But unlike the broader “dancing mania” that was taking place across Europe at the same time, this dance, dubbed the “tarantella,” was more than a sickness. It was also a cure.

“Some people say that the bite of a spider caused people to tremor and shake,” Anna Harsh, a professional dancer and founder of the Allegro Dance Company, which specializes in Italian folk dances, tells Popular Science. They’d then continue moving to sweat out the poison.

Tarantism, a historical psychological and social phenomenon that led to anxiety, melancholia, and uncontrollable movement, ran rapidly throughout southern Italy from the 11th to the 17th century.

The epicenter of tarantism was Taranto, a coastal city in southern Italy’s Puglia region, which occupies the “heel” of the country’s boot shape. Each summer harvest season, local residents would spend long days working in the fields where large, hairy wolf spiders burrowed.

Recent findings suggest that most people believed that these wolf spiders carried a toxic venom. If they bit you, tarantism would quickly set in. The only cure would be to sweat out the venom through continuous, fast-paced dancing. We’re talking uncontrollable, flailing movements that would eventually exhaust both the dancer and the illness.

Although southern Italy was the epicenter of tarantism, similar outbreaks of involuntary, convulsive dancing occurred throughout the Middle Ages. The first major recorded frenzy began on June 24, 1374 in Aachen, Germany. Soon after, others followed in countries like Switzerland and modern-day France. In many of these cases, those afflicted danced uncontrollably for days or weeks. Some even died dancing. Since these events happened centuries ago, no one really knows what caused them. But the tarantism of southern Italy and its ensuing tarantella dance both seem unique.

According to recent reports, the name “tarantula” may have originated with the wolf spiders (Lycosa tarantula) of Taranto, but wolf spiders and tarantulas belong to two entirely different spider families. Still, with a leg span that can reach up to three to four inches across, multiple sets of eyes, and a series of odd, jerky movements when they walk, wolf spiders make easy targets for conspiracy theories and urban legends.

It has been revealed that while they can look frightening, science has determined over the years that a wolf spider’s bite is generally harmless to humans. Symptoms appear more like a mild bee sting, with a bit of localized pain and swelling, then a full-blown disco dance party. In fact, among the world’s 38,000 known spider species, only about 100 species have venom that is detrimental to humans.

In 1976, a college paper blamed the Salem witch trials on moldy bread. It wasn’t true.

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy.

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution.

4 times drinking coffee was illegal—or even punishable by death.

The mysterious dancing plague that killed people in 1518.

The radioactive ‘miracle water’ that killed its believers.

Recent findings suggest that in August 1693, an anonymous Neapolitan doctor even tested the connection between the bite of a wolf spider and tarantism. He let two wolf spiders bite him in a public experiment, but the doctor never broke out into fancy footwork.

Instead, modern science highlights that the extreme summer heat, physical stress, dehydration, and even ample wine drinking could have easily caused the symptoms of tarantism. Still, the wolf spider and tarantism remain undisputedly linked.

Industry observers note that sometimes called the “Dance of the Spider,” the tarantella began as a ritual healing dance that aimed to sweat out any venom associated with tarantism. Many versions of the tarantella exist today, though they’re more traditional folk dances than medical treatments. Instead, the  ‘tarantella as cure’ dance is more formally known as the pizzica. The word pizzica comes from the Italian verb pizzicare, which means “to pinch” or “to bite.”.

“Today we might think of that ‘bite’ as something internal, like stress or anxiety,” states Harsh. Picture when someone you know suddenly loses a loved one and they’re shaking uncontrollably. “That person will dance or move and do whatever they can to help them get through that situation.”.

Pizzica tarantata is performed almost like an exorcism, the spiritual practice of evicting demons or malevolent entities (such as supposed spider’s venom) through a sort of ritual—in this case, ecstatic, free-form dance.

Musicians gathered around the inflicted victim, playing incessant, fast-paced 6/8-tempo rhythms driven by a tambourine, violins, and guitars. The person suffering from tarantism would then “go into a trance,” says Harsh. “There was shaking, hopping, swirling, and turning. Some people would roll on the ground and come back up. The pizzica has movements, but you can put them in any order. It’s however the spirit moves you.”.

It has been revealed that these days, most historians and scientists agree that wolf spiders didn’t cause tarantism. Rather, tarantism was a form of mass hysteria, a situation where a group of people share the same intense fear, anxiety, or physical sickness—like dizziness, shaking, or stomach aches—even though there is no real physical or medical grounds for it.

According to recent reports, tarantism mostly afflicted impoverished individuals, particularly women (tarantatas). One possible reason: “Women were oppressed and faced plenty of inequality,” states Harsh. “Dance is a way that they could express themselves, even scream, through movement. That they could be the center of attention for just a minute and be seen.”.

Over the centuries, the tarantella has become a celebration of life and joy rather than a frantic ritual. Italians often perform this now-beloved folk dance at weddings and festivals.

Every August, La Notte della Taranta, Europe’s largest open-air festival dedicated to traditional folk music, the pizzica, and the tarantella, takes place in Italy’s Puglia region.

Whether or not dancing works to sweat out a toxic venom, studies do show that dancing helps reduce stress and increases levels of serotonin, a hormone that helps regulate mood, sleep, and digestion.

It has been revealed that “You know, whatever is biting at us, whether it’s grief or loss, we can move together, follow the rhythm of a drummer, and heal ourselves in a sense,” says Harsh. “The movement just takes over and we stop thinking about our troubles.”.

Though if you do endure a lethal spider bite, we’d recommend the ER over two-stepping.
